metadata.title: BMR Calculator

faqs.question: What is BMR?
faqs.answer: Basal metabolic rate is the number of calories your body needs at complete rest to maintain basic functions like breathing, circulation, and cell production. It typically accounts for 60-75% of daily energy expenditure.

faqs.question: Which BMR formula is best?
faqs.answer: Mifflin-St Jeor is considered the most accurate for most people. Harris-Benedict tends to slightly overestimate. If you know your body fat percentage, Katch-McArdle is best.

faqs.question: How is BMR different from TDEE?
faqs.answer: BMR is calories at rest. TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) = BMR × activity factor. TDEE includes all daily activity and exercise. Use TDEE for calorie planning, not BMR alone.

metadata.title: Waist-to-Hip Ratio Calculator
metadata.description: Assess health risk according to the WHO waist-to-hip ratio standards.

faqs.question: What is the waist-to-hip ratio?
faqs.answer: Waist-to-hip ratio = waist circumference ÷ hip circumference. It measures fat distribution. Higher ratios (more abdominal fat) are associated with increased health risks for heart disease, diabetes, and stroke.

faqs.question: What is a healthy waist-to-hip ratio?
faqs.answer: WHO guidelines: men should stay below 0.90 and women below 0.80. Ratios above 1.0 (men) or 0.85 (women) indicate significantly elevated health risk.

faqs.question: How do I measure correctly?
faqs.answer: Waist: measure at the narrowest point between the ribs and hip bones (usually at the navel). Hips: measure at the widest part of the buttocks. Keep the tape horizontal, snug but not tight.

faqs.question: How much water should I drink per day?
faqs.answer: A general guideline is about 35 ml per kilogram of body weight (roughly half your weight in ounces). Active people and those in hot climates need more. The '8 glasses of water a day' rule is a rough estimate.

faqs.question: Does coffee count toward my water intake?
faqs.answer: Mostly yes. Although caffeine is a mild diuretic, the water in coffee and tea still contributes to hydration. However, plain water remains the best source.

faqs.question: How do I know if I'm well hydrated?
faqs.answer: Check your urine color — pale yellow indicates good hydration. Dark yellow means you need to drink more water. Other signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, headache, and fatigue.

faqs.question: What is a 1RM?
faqs.answer: Your one-rep max (1RM) is the maximum weight you can lift with proper form. It is used to set training percentages and track strength progress.

faqs.question: Which 1RM formula is most accurate?
faqs.answer: Brzycki and Epley are the most commonly used and tend to be accurate for 1-10 reps. All formulas become less accurate above 10 reps. For best accuracy, test with a weight you can lift 3-5 times.

faqs.question: How do I train using my 1RM?
faqs.answer: Common training zones: Strength: 80-90%, 3-5 reps. Hypertrophy: 65-80%, 8-12 reps. Endurance: 50-65%, 15-20 reps. Power: 50-70%, 3-6 explosive reps.

metadata.title: Annuity Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate the present and future value of an annuity, supporting ordinary and annuity due.

faqs.question: What is an annuity and how does it work?
faqs.answer: An annuity is a financial contract between you and an insurance company. During the accumulation phase, you invest money that grows tax-deferred. During the payout (annuitization) phase, the insurer pays you a regular income stream. Annuities are commonly used for retirement planning to guarantee income you cannot outlive.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a fixed and variable annuity?
faqs.answer: A fixed annuity offers a guaranteed interest rate and predictable growth, making it lower risk. A variable annuity invests in sub-accounts similar to mutual funds, so returns fluctuate with the market. Variable annuities have higher growth potential but also more risk. This calculator models both so you can compare projected outcomes.

faqs.question: How does tax-deferred growth benefit an annuity?
faqs.answer: In a tax-deferred annuity, you don't pay taxes on investment gains each year. This lets your entire balance compound without tax drag. Over decades, this advantage can be substantial. For example, at a 6% return and 25% tax rate over 20 years, tax deferral can result in tens of thousands of dollars more in your account compared to a taxable investment.

faqs.question: How is my annuity payout amount calculated?
faqs.answer: Payout amounts are calculated using the present value of an annuity formula: PMT = PV x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n), where PV is your account balance, r is the interest rate per period, and n is the total number of payment periods. This ensures your balance is fully distributed over the chosen payout period while continuing to earn interest.

faqs.question: When should I consider buying an annuity?
faqs.answer: Annuities are worth considering if you've maxed out other tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA), want guaranteed retirement income, or are concerned about outliving your savings. They work best as part of a diversified retirement strategy. Deferred annuities are most effective when purchased 10-30 years before retirement to maximize tax-deferred compounding.

faqs.question: What fees are typically associated with annuities?
faqs.answer: Common annuity fees include mortality and expense charges (1-1.5%), administrative fees, fund management fees for variable annuities (0.5-2%), and surrender charges for early withdrawal (typically 5-10% declining over 5-10 years). This calculator shows gross returns before fees. Subtract roughly 1-2.5% from the interest rate to estimate after-fee performance for variable annuities.

metadata.title: Blood Alcohol Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate blood alcohol concentration (BAC) based on drinks, weight, gender, and time.

faqs.question: How does the Widmark formula calculate BAC?
faqs.answer: The Widmark formula estimates BAC as: BAC = (grams of alcohol consumed / (body weight in grams x Widmark r factor)) - (0.015 x hours since first drink). The Widmark r factor accounts for differences in body water distribution between genders (0.68 for men, 0.55 for women). The 0.015 rate represents the average hourly elimination rate of alcohol.

faqs.question: What is a standard drink in the U.S.?
faqs.answer: A U.S. standard drink contains about 14 grams (0.6 fluid ounces) of pure alcohol. This is roughly equivalent to 12 ounces of regular beer (5% ABV), 5 ounces of wine (12% ABV), or 1.5 ounces of distilled spirits (40% ABV / 80 proof). Many cocktails and craft beers contain more than one standard drink.

faqs.question: Is this BAC calculator accurate?
faqs.answer: This calculator provides only a rough estimate. Actual BAC is influenced by many factors not considered here, including food intake, medications, liver health, hydration status, individual metabolism, genetics, and body composition. Two people of the same weight and gender can have very different BACs after drinking the same amount. Never rely on a calculator to judge whether it is safe to drive.

faqs.question: What BAC level is considered drunk driving?
faqs.answer: In the U.S., the legal driving limit for drivers aged 21 and over in all 50 states is 0.08% BAC. Commercial drivers (CDL holders) have a lower limit of 0.04%. Drivers under 21 face zero-tolerance laws, typically 0.00-0.02% depending on the state. Many countries have lower limits, such as 0.05% in Australia and most of Europe.

faqs.question: How long does alcohol take to leave the body?
faqs.answer: On average, the body eliminates alcohol at a rate of about 0.015% BAC per hour, roughly equal to one standard drink per hour. However, this rate varies from person to person. A person with a BAC of 0.08% would need about 5.3 hours to reach 0.00%. There is no way to speed up the process; coffee, cold showers, and exercise will not lower BAC faster.

faqs.question: Why does body weight affect BAC?
faqs.answer: Alcohol distributes through body water. Larger people typically have more body water to dilute the alcohol, resulting in a lower BAC for the same amount of alcohol. This is also why the Widmark factor differs by gender: men generally have a higher body water percentage (68%) than women (55%), meaning the same amount of alcohol at the same weight typically produces a higher BAC in women.

faqs.question: Can I use this calculator to know if it is safe to drive?
faqs.answer: No. This calculator is for educational and informational purposes only. The rough estimate it provides can differ significantly from your actual BAC. Impairment can occur even below legal limits. The only safe amount of alcohol to consume before driving is zero. If you have been drinking, use a designated driver, ride-share service, or taxi.

faqs.question: What is a calorie deficit?
faqs.answer: A calorie deficit means consuming fewer calories than your body burns (TDEE). A daily deficit of 500 calories can lead to about 1 pound of fat loss per week (3,500 calories = 1 pound).

faqs.question: How large should the deficit be?
faqs.answer: A 500-calorie daily deficit (1 pound per week) is sustainable for most people. Deficits over 1,000 calories per day may lead to muscle loss, fatigue, and a slowed metabolism. Don't go below 1,200 calories per day without medical supervision.

faqs.question: Why am I not losing weight despite a deficit?
faqs.answer: Common causes: underestimating portion sizes, not tracking cooking oils or drinks, water retention masking fat loss, or metabolic adaptation. Try accurately re-measuring your food intake for 1-2 weeks.

metadata.title: Car Lease Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate monthly lease payments, money factor, and total lease cost.

faqs.question: What is a money factor in car leasing?
faqs.answer: The money factor is the lease equivalent of an interest rate, expressed as a decimal (e.g., 0.0025). To convert to APR, multiply by 2,400. A lower money factor means lower financing costs.

faqs.question: How is the monthly lease payment calculated?
faqs.answer: Monthly lease payment = (Depreciation + Rent Charge) × Tax. Depreciation = (Negotiated Price - Residual Value) / Term. Rent Charge = (Negotiated Price + Residual Value) × Money Factor.

faqs.question: What is residual value?
faqs.answer: Residual value is the estimated worth of the vehicle at lease end, set by the leasing company. It's typically 50-60% of MSRP for a 3-year lease. Higher residual means lower monthly payments.

faqs.question: Should I lease or buy?
faqs.answer: Leasing is better if you drive less than 15,000 miles/year, want lower monthly payments, and prefer driving a new car every 2-3 years. Buying is better if you drive a lot, plan to keep the car long-term, or want to build equity.

faqs.question: Can I negotiate the lease price?
faqs.answer: Yes. The negotiated price (cap cost) is negotiable just like a purchase price. Lower negotiated price means lower monthly payments. Research invoice prices and negotiate before discussing lease terms.

faqs.question: What fees are included in a lease?
faqs.answer: Typical lease fees include acquisition fee, disposition fee, excess mileage charges, and wear-and-tear fees. This calculator focuses on monthly payments. Ask the dealer for a complete fee breakdown.

faqs.question: What is the difference between straight-line and double declining balance?
faqs.answer: Straight-line depreciation is the same every year and simple to calculate. Double declining balance is an accelerated method: higher depreciation in early years and less later, matching how equipment loses value quickly.

faqs.question: What is salvage value?
faqs.answer: Salvage value is the estimated remaining value of an asset at the end of its useful life. It must be lower than the asset cost. Total depreciation = Cost − Salvage value.

faqs.question: Which method is better for taxes?
faqs.answer: Tax rules vary by region. Straight-line is widely accepted and simple. Accelerated methods (like double declining balance) are used for certain asset classes in some countries - consult a tax professional.

faqs.question: What does the results table include?
faqs.answer: The table shows the annual depreciation and ending book value for both methods year by year, making it easy to compare and prepare depreciation details.

faqs.answer: Monthly payment = (Depreciation + Rent Charge) × (1 + Tax Rate). Depreciation = (Price − Residual Value) ÷ Term, and Rent Charge = (Price + Residual Value) × Money Factor.

faqs.question: What is the residual value percentage?
faqs.answer: Residual value is the estimated remaining value of the asset at the end of the lease, usually entered as a percentage of the price. The higher the residual value, the lower the monthly payment.

faqs.question: How do I convert an annual interest rate to a money factor?
faqs.answer: Money factor = Annual rate (%) ÷ 2400. For example, a 4.5% annual rate equals a money factor of 0.001875.

metadata.title: Present Value Calculator
metadata.description: Free online calculator to compute present value, discount factor, and interest amount from future value, annual rate, years, and compounding frequency.

faqs.question: What is present value?
faqs.answer: Present value is what a future amount is worth today at a given discount rate: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r/m)^(m×t).

faqs.question: What is a discount factor?
faqs.answer: Discount factor = 1 ÷ (1 + r/m)^(m×t), representing how much 1 dollar in the future is worth today. The larger the factor, the lower the discount rate or the shorter the term.

faqs.question: How does compounding frequency affect the result?
faqs.answer: The more frequent the compounding (e.g., monthly vs yearly), the stronger the discounting effect at the same nominal rate, so the lower the present value.

faqs.question: What is present value used for?
faqs.answer: It is used for investment valuation, bond pricing, discounting project cash flows (DCF), and comparing the value of money at different points in time.

faqs.question: How does this calculator compare renting and buying?
faqs.answer: It simulates both paths year by year: the renter invests the money saved at a set return rate, while the buyer builds home equity (appreciation minus the remaining loan). The year when both net worths are equal is the break-even point.

faqs.question: What is the break-even year?
faqs.answer: The break-even year is the first year the buyer's net worth exceeds the renter's. Before that, renting plus investing is better; after that, buying is better. It is typically 5-10 years.

faqs.question: Why count investment returns for the renter?
faqs.answer: It reflects opportunity cost: the down payment and monthly payment difference could have been invested. Including it makes the comparison of real wealth accumulation fair for both sides.

faqs.question: Which assumptions affect the result most?
faqs.answer: Home appreciation, property tax rate, and annual rent growth have the biggest impact and vary greatly by city. Adjust them to local market data.

faqs.question: How is dog age converted to human age?
faqs.answer: This tool uses a scientific formula: the first two years equal about 24 human years, then each year adds roughly 16×ln(dog age)+31, with adjustments for breed size.

faqs.question: Why does breed size affect the conversion?
faqs.answer: Small breeds mature faster but age more slowly overall; large breeds are the opposite. So at the same dog age, large breeds have a higher human age.

faqs.question: Is the "dog age × 7" rule accurate?
faqs.answer: No. The "×7" rule is just a rough rule of thumb that ignores early development speed and size differences. The logarithmic formula is much closer to real biology.

faqs.question: How do I use the comparison chart?

metadata.title: CD Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate CD interest and maturity value with compounding frequency and taxes.

faqs.question: What is a Certificate of Deposit (CD) and how does it work?
faqs.answer: A Certificate of Deposit is a savings product offered by banks and credit unions where you deposit money for a fixed period (the term) at a guaranteed interest rate. In exchange for locking up your money, you typically earn a higher interest rate than a regular savings account. When the CD matures (reaches the end of its term), you receive your original deposit plus all accrued interest. Terms range from as short as 1 month to as long as 10 years.

faqs.question: What is the difference between APY and APR for CDs?
faqs.answer: APY (Annual Percentage Yield) reflects the total amount of interest you earn in a year including the effect of compounding. APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the simple interest rate without compounding factored in. Because CDs compound interest, the APY is always slightly higher than the APR. Banks are required to advertise APY, making it easier to compare offers. For example, a 5.00% APR compounded daily yields an APY of approximately 5.13%.

faqs.question: What is a CD ladder strategy and why should I use one?
faqs.answer: A CD ladder involves splitting your total investment across multiple CDs with staggered maturity dates (e.g., 1-year, 2-year, 3-year, 4-year, and 5-year CDs). As each shorter-term CD matures, you can reinvest it at the longest term to capture higher rates, or access the cash if needed. This strategy balances liquidity with higher long-term rates, reducing the risk of locking all your money away at a single rate while still earning more than a savings account.

faqs.question: What are typical early withdrawal penalties for CDs?
faqs.answer: Early withdrawal penalties vary by bank and CD term. Common penalties include 3 months of interest for CDs with terms under 1 year, 6 months of interest for 1-year CDs, and 12 months or more of interest for longer-term CDs. Some banks charge a flat fee instead. In extreme cases, the penalty can eat into your principal if you withdraw very early. Always check your bank's specific penalty terms before opening a CD.

faqs.question: How does compounding frequency affect my CD earnings?
faqs.answer: Compounding frequency determines how often earned interest is added to your balance to earn additional interest. Daily compounding yields the most because interest is calculated and added every day. Monthly, quarterly, and annual compounding produce progressively less total interest. However, the differences are relatively small. For example, on a $10,000 CD at 5% APY for 1 year, the difference between daily and annual compounding is typically only a few dollars.

faqs.question: Are CDs safe? Is my money insured?
faqs.answer: CDs from FDIC-insured banks are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Credit union CDs (called share certificates) are similarly insured by the NCUA. This makes CDs one of the safest investment options available. The trade-off is that CD rates are generally lower than potential stock market returns, but your principal is guaranteed and the interest rate is locked in for the term.

faqs.question: When is the best time to open a CD?
faqs.answer: The best time to open a CD is when interest rates are high relative to historical norms, or when you expect rates to decline. Locking in a high rate before the Federal Reserve cuts rates means you benefit from that rate for the entire CD term. If rates are expected to rise, shorter-term CDs or a CD ladder strategy lets you reinvest at higher rates as they become available.

metadata.title: EMI Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate equated monthly installments, total interest, and generate an amortization schedule.

faqs.question: What is EMI and how is it calculated?
faqs.answer: EMI stands for Equated Monthly Installment. It is the fixed amount you pay every month to repay your loan. The formula is EMI = P x r x (1+r)^n / [(1+r)^n - 1], where P is the principal loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate divided by 12), and n is the total number of monthly installments. This calculator computes EMI instantly for any loan amount, interest rate, and tenure.

faqs.question: How does prepayment affect my loan?
faqs.answer: Prepayment — whether as extra monthly payments or a one-time lump sum — goes directly toward reducing your outstanding principal. This lowers the interest charged in subsequent months, which can significantly reduce total interest paid and shorten your loan tenure. Even small additional monthly payments can save thousands over the life of a loan.

faqs.question: What is an amortization schedule?
faqs.answer: An amortization schedule is a table showing every payment over the life of a loan, broken down into principal and interest components. Early payments are mostly interest, while later payments are mostly principal. This calculator provides both a month-by-month and year-by-year amortization schedule so you can see exactly how your loan balance decreases over time.

faqs.question: Can I compare multiple loan offers with this calculator?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Loan Comparison tab lets you enter up to three different loan offers with varying amounts, interest rates, and tenures. The calculator shows EMI, total interest, and total payment for each offer side by side, making it easy to pick the most cost-effective option.

faqs.question: Does a longer tenure mean I pay more interest?
faqs.answer: Yes. A longer loan tenure lowers your monthly EMI, making it more affordable month-to-month, but you pay significantly more in total interest. For example, a $500,000 loan at 8.5% costs about $230,000 in interest over 15 years but over $420,000 over 30 years. Always weigh monthly affordability against total cost when choosing a tenure.

faqs.question: Is this EMI calculator accurate for all loan types?
faqs.answer: This calculator is accurate for any fixed-rate loan with equal monthly installments, including home loans, car loans, personal loans, and education loans. It does not account for variable interest rates, processing fees, or insurance premiums, which may affect your actual repayment amount.

metadata.title: Future Value Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate the future value of investments with regular contributions and compounding frequency.

faqs.question: What is future value and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on a given rate of return. It matters because it helps you understand how much your savings or investments will grow over time, enabling better financial planning for goals like retirement, education, or major purchases.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an ordinary annuity and an annuity due?
faqs.answer: An ordinary annuity makes payments at the end of each period (e.g., most bond coupon payments), while an annuity due makes payments at the beginning of each period (e.g., rent or insurance premiums). An annuity due grows slightly more because each payment has one extra period to earn interest.

faqs.question: How does compounding frequency affect future value?
faqs.answer: More frequent compounding (monthly vs. annually) produces a higher future value because interest begins earning interest sooner. For example, $10,000 at 6% compounded monthly yields more than 6% compounded annually over the same period. The difference becomes more pronounced at higher rates and longer time horizons.

faqs.question: What is the future value formula for a lump sum?
faqs.answer: The future value of a lump sum is calculated as FV = PV x (1 + r/n)^(n*t), where PV is the present value, r is the annual interest rate, n is the number of compounding periods per year, and t is the number of years. This formula accounts for compound interest on the initial investment.

faqs.question: Why should I adjust future value for inflation?
faqs.answer: Inflation erodes purchasing power over time. A dollar today buys more than a dollar 20 years from now. Adjusting for inflation (using the real rate of return) shows your investment's future value in today's purchasing power, giving you a more realistic picture of what your money will actually be worth.

faqs.question: What is a growth multiplier?
faqs.answer: The growth multiplier shows how many times your total contributions have multiplied through compound interest. For example, a growth multiplier of 1.5x means your investment grew to 1.5 times what you put in. A multiplier above 2x means you earned more in interest than you contributed.

faqs.question: What are heart rate zones?
faqs.answer: Heart rate zones divide effort into 5 levels based on a percentage of your maximum heart rate. Each zone trains a different energy system — from easy recovery (Zone 1) to maximal effort sprints (Zone 5).

faqs.question: What is the Karvonen method?
faqs.answer: Karvonen uses your heart rate reserve (max heart rate - resting heart rate) for more personalized zones. It accounts for your fitness level through your resting heart rate and is more accurate than simple percentages of max heart rate.

faqs.question: How do I find my resting heart rate?
faqs.answer: Measure your pulse before getting out of bed in the morning for 3 consecutive days. Count beats for 60 seconds. Take the average. Typical resting heart rate: 60-80 bpm (athletes: 40-60).

faqs.question: What is ideal body weight?
faqs.answer: Ideal body weight is an estimated healthy weight range based on height and gender. Four common formulas (Devine, Robinson, Miller, Hamwi) give slightly different results. Use the average as a general guideline.

faqs.question: Are ideal weight formulas accurate?
faqs.answer: These formulas are rough estimates and do not account for muscle mass, bone density, or body composition. A muscular person may weigh more than the ideal weight yet still be very healthy. Use the BMI range as a supplementary metric.

faqs.question: How do I know my body frame size?
faqs.answer: Wrap your thumb and index finger around your wrist. If they overlap: small frame. If they touch: medium frame. If they don't touch: large frame. You can also measure your wrist circumference — less than 6.5 inches indicates a small frame.

faqs.question: What is the ketogenic diet?
faqs.answer: The keto diet is very low in carbs (usually 20-50g net carbs per day), moderate in protein, and high in fat. This shifts your body into ketosis, burning fat instead of carbs for fuel.

faqs.question: How many carbs can I eat on keto?
faqs.answer: Most people enter ketosis at under 20-25g net carbs per day. Some can go as high as 50g and stay in ketosis. Net carbs = total carbs minus fiber. Start at 20g and adjust based on results.

faqs.question: How much protein do I need on keto?
faqs.answer: Aim for 1.2-2.0g per kg of body weight. Too little protein leads to muscle loss. Contrary to popular belief, moderate-to-high protein won't kick you out of ketosis.

metadata.title: Markup Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate markup, profit margin, and selling price, with batch support for multiple products.

faqs.question: What is markup and how is it calculated?
faqs.answer: Markup is the percentage added to the cost of a product to determine its selling price. The formula is: Markup % = ((Selling Price - Cost) / Cost) x 100. For example, if a product costs $50 and you sell it for $80, the markup is ((80 - 50) / 50) x 100 = 60%.

faqs.question: What is the difference between markup and profit margin?
faqs.answer: Markup is calculated as a percentage of cost, while profit margin is calculated as a percentage of the selling price (revenue). A 100% markup equals a 50% profit margin. Markup is always higher than margin for the same transaction because cost is a smaller base than revenue. Both measure profitability but from different perspectives.

faqs.question: How do I convert markup to margin?
faqs.answer: To convert markup to margin, use the formula: Margin % = (Markup % / (100 + Markup %)) x 100. For example, a 50% markup converts to (50 / 150) x 100 = 33.33% margin. To convert margin to markup: Markup % = (Margin % / (100 - Margin %)) x 100.

faqs.question: What is a typical markup percentage for retail?
faqs.answer: Markup varies widely by industry. Grocery stores typically use 10-30% markup, clothing retail 100-300%, electronics 30-50%, restaurants 200-400% on food, and jewelry 100-400%. The ideal markup depends on operating costs, competition, perceived value, and demand elasticity.

faqs.question: How do I calculate selling price from cost and markup?
faqs.answer: Multiply the cost by (1 + markup percentage / 100). For example, if your cost is $40 and you want a 75% markup: $40 x (1 + 0.75) = $40 x 1.75 = $70 selling price. The gross profit would be $70 - $40 = $30.

faqs.question: Can markup percentage be over 100%?
faqs.answer: Yes, a markup over 100% is common in many industries. A 100% markup means you sell an item for double its cost. A 200% markup means the selling price is three times the cost. Restaurants, for example, often apply 200-400% markup on beverages and food items.

faqs.question: How do I find cost from selling price and markup?
faqs.answer: Divide the selling price by (1 + markup percentage / 100). For example, if the selling price is $120 and the markup is 50%: $120 / (1 + 0.50) = $120 / 1.50 = $80 cost. This is useful for reverse-engineering competitor pricing.

faqs.question: What is the difference between mean, median, and mode?
faqs.answer: The mean is the average (sum ÷ count). The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the most frequent value. They are similar for symmetric data but can differ significantly for skewed data.

faqs.question: When should I use the median instead of the mean?
faqs.answer: Use the median when data has outliers or is skewed (like income data). The median is resistant to extreme values. For example, if most people earn $50,000 but one person earns $10 million, the median better represents the typical value.

faqs.question: Can there be multiple modes?
faqs.answer: Yes. If two values tie as most frequent, the data is bimodal. If all values occur equally often, there is no mode.
